newsitem.title: ROMANIA: ROMANIA GOVERNMENT APPROVES HEALTH INSURANCE BILL.
newsitem.headline: ROMANIA GOVERNMENT APPROVES HEALTH INSURANCE BILL.

text.p: Romania's centrist coalition government on Friday approved a long-delayed health insurance bill, seen as a major step to reform the Balkan country's underfunded medical sector, a government official said.
"This bill will descentralise and introduce competition in the health system," Health Ministry state secretary Ioan Romosanu told journalists.
Under the bill, the present centralised administration of the health insurance budget would be replaced by independent Health insurance funds (CAS).
"The bill will allow CAS to chose any hospital which it thinks it can offer the best services," Romosanu said.
Under the present regulations, patients are registered at hospitals located in the area of their residence.
The draft needs parliament endorsement to become effective.
The bill would also allow Romanian tax payers access to private "luxury" services in exchange of an extra insurance quota administered by private funds, he said.
Since the 1989 collapse of communism, health care has virtually collapsed under bad management, misuse of funds, lack of medicines and equipment, underpaid staff and overcrowded hospitals.
Under the bill, distribution of funds to hospitals and medical staff would be proportionate with the number of patients.
"Wages in the health sector will no longer be fixed ones. They will reflect the quality of the work according to the principle: no clients, no money," Romosanu said.
Experienced Romanian doctors earn the equivalent of some $70 a month.
Reports in the local media said bribing medical staff has become common practice in the Balkan country.

Poverty, malnutrition and poor hygiene have reduced life expectancy and led to a comeback of such illnesses as viral meningitis, typhoid and cholera. Tuberculosis, cancer and veneral diseases are on the rise and the country is afflicted by 54 percent of Europe's juvenile AIDS cases.
